analysis.one_liner: Adds dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and boosts federal Medicaid funding for those services.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare currently excludes routine dental care, eyeglasses, and hearing aids, so millions of seniors pay out of pocket or go without. This bill would add coverage for dental cleanings, fillings, root canals, dentures, eye exams, glasses and contacts, hearing exams, and hearing aids, with limits like one denture set every five years and one hearing aid per ear every four years. It would also raise the federal share of Medicaid costs for dental, vision, and hearing services to 90 percent, easing the burden on states.
analysis.who_benefits: Older adults on Medicare, who today generally pay full price for dentists, glasses, and hearing aids, and adults covered by Medicaid in states that choose to expand these services with the richer federal match.

how_it_helps.text: Adds Medicare coverage of routine dental cleanings and exams, basic services like fillings and crowns, major services like root canals and extractions, emergency dental care, and dentures [S2][S3].
Adds Medicare coverage of routine eye exams, eyeglass lenses and frames, contact lenses, and low-vision devices [S2][S3].
Adds Medicare coverage of routine hearing exams and hearing aids, repealing the statutory exclusion that currently bars payment for them [S2][S3].
Raises the federal Medicaid matching rate to 90 percent for dental, vision, and hearing services furnished to adults, reducing the cost to states of covering those services [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund the new Medicare benefit and 90 percent of state Medicaid spending on these services; the bill text contains no offsetting tax or spending change to pay for it.

drawbacks.text: The bill includes no financing mechanism, so the full cost of the new Medicare benefit and the 90 percent Medicaid match would add to the federal deficit [S3].

Medicare payment for the new services starts at 0 percent of the payment amount in the first year and ramps up only 10 percentage points a year, reaching 80 percent in year eight, which could leave patients with substantial out-of-pocket costs during the phase-in and could make providers reluctant to serve Medicare patients at the low early rates [S3].
The Secretary of Health and Human Services is given broad authority to impose additional limits, including prior authorization, which could narrow the benefit in practice [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and targeted at a real gap: Medicare's exclusion of dental, vision, and hearing care forces seniors to pay out of pocket or go without, and untreated dental and hearing problems carry real health costs. The honest counterweight is money: the bill is an open-ended new federal entitlement with no dedicated funding and a slow phase-in under which Medicare would cover little in the early years. A fully designed version would need a financing source and a faster ramp-up.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended, so it never came up for a vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Bob Casey introduced the bill on March 16, 2023, joined by five Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Cardin, Brown, Blumenthal, Fetterman, and Welch [S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced [S5][S1].
The action history shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome leaves the status quo intact: the federal government avoids the cost of a new entitlement with no funding source, while Medicare beneficiaries continue paying market prices for dental, vision, and hearing care, and dental, optical, and hearing-aid providers keep selling to them largely outside insurance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: taxpayers spared cost, seniors still pay

for.name: Sen. Bob Casey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to add dental, vision, and hearing coverage to Medicare and Medicaid.

for.name: 6 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing or markup — for the remaining twenty-two months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters — the sponsor and his cosponsors — were Democrats; no Senate Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where a broader partisan split could be measured.

industries.note: Medicare coverage would make tens of millions of seniors paying dental patients, though the bill's slow payment ramp-up to 80 percent would limit how much practices collect early on.
Repealing Medicare's statutory exclusion for hearing aids would create a large insured market for hearing aids and audiology visits, capped at one aid per ear every four years.
Coverage of eye exams, glasses, and contact lenses (with a $200 per-24-month contact lens cap) would turn routine vision care into an insured service.
A 90 percent federal match for adult dental, vision, and hearing services would shift most of the cost of these Medicaid benefits from states to the federal government.
